title: My Team Was Doing Their Jobs Perfectly The Problem Was Me
author: Mulder, Summer
summary: Mulder shares a critical moment of leadership clarity and growth: realizing her high-performing team's interpersonal friction and challenges stemmed not from their capabilities or intentions but from her own leadership approach, expectations, and way of engaging with them. The team wasn't the problem—their leader's expectations, communication style, and approach were creating unnecessary friction and preventing them from thriving. This realization led to significant behavioral changes that transformed team dynamics. The story illustrates how often leadership problems are leadership problems.
points: When teams are underperforming, the first place to look is your own leadership, not their capability.
Team friction often comes from leader expectations and communication, not team incompetence.
Leadership clarity requires ruthless honesty about your own role in team dynamics.
High-performing teams can still struggle under leadership that isn't aligned with their needs.
Changing your leadership approach is often more impactful than changing team members.
The best leaders own their role in team dysfunction before blaming their people.
quotes: My team was doing their jobs perfectly. The problem was me, not them.
I looked at their performance and realized the issue wasn't their capability—it was my expectations.
The moment I saw my role in the team's struggle, everything changed.
Team friction that seems like a people problem is often a leadership problem.
Some of the highest-performing people can struggle under leadership that doesn't fit them.
Changing my approach as a leader was more powerful than any change in team composition.
When leaders own their role in problems, team dynamics transform almost immediately.
The humility to see yourself as the problem is what allows real team transformation.
My team didn't need to change; I needed to change how I was leading them.
Great leaders are willing to be the problem so their team can stop being blamed for it.” Archived from Substack (Summer Mulder) on May 2, 2026 by Tim.
